description: Selected edited excerpts of Johnny Meintel homelab investigations. Original statuses and classifications retained; raw evidence, private links and original record fingerprints omitted. This is not the live incident queue.

records.labRunId: N/A (planned hands-on test, lab log LABLOG-2026-10-04 section 1)
records.alertSource: Wazuh rule 100343 via Splunk and LabWatch
records.title: FakeCorp portal: repeated failed logins investigated
records.initialAlert: Wazuh rule 100343 detected six failed portal logins from the same lab workstation within 120 seconds. The rule fired at level 10; the case retains its recorded Informational severity.
records.observedFacts: Johnny deliberately generated failed logins against the synthetic FakeCorp portal and reviewed the resulting Wazuh and Splunk records. The single-event failure rule fired before the repeated-failure rule created this incident.
records.scope: Controlled authentication test from WS02 to the FakeCorp portal on SRV01. This was not an external intrusion.
records.attribution: Johnny performed the hands-on test and investigation. Claude Code later moved the resolved case to Closed at his request, preserving his analysis.
records.impact: Expected failed logins against synthetic lab accounts. This case does not establish a compromised account.
records.timeline:
October 6: Johnny generated the failed logins and investigated the threshold alert.
October 13: Claude Code completed the requested workflow transition to Closed.
records.evidence: Private source records: FakeCorp authentication log, Wazuh 100343 alert and corresponding Splunk event. Raw records and attachments are not published in this excerpt.
records.queries: Compare the source address, account field, failure sequence and timestamps across the application log and SIEM records. Review the account spread before calling a pattern a spray.
records.detection: The single failure and repeated-failure rules behaved differently as intended. The threshold event became a LabWatch case.
records.containment: No emergency containment was required for this authorized test.
records.recovery: No service recovery was required for the detection test.
records.conclusion: Expected Test Activity. Johnny verified that repeated failed logins produced the intended alert and incident.
records.validation: The observed failure sequence, threshold alert and LabWatch case were correlated. This validates the tested case, not every authentication scenario.
records.lessons: One failed login can be a typo. Repeated failures need context: source, accounts, timing and whether any login succeeded.
records.publicWorkCredit: Johnny performed the hands-on test and investigation. Claude Code later moved the resolved case to Closed at his request, preserving his analysis.

records.alertSource: Wazuh rule 100345 via Splunk and LabWatch
records.title: FakeCorp portal: successful SQL-injection login investigated
records.initialAlert: Wazuh rule 100345 detected a successful portal login whose email field contained SQL-like input. The rule fired at level 12; the case retains its recorded Informational severity.
records.observedFacts: Johnny entered SQL-injection test input in the deliberately vulnerable login form. The login succeeded and rule 100345 fired. He reviewed the application and SIEM evidence.
records.scope: FakeCorp portal on SRV01, using synthetic lab data. No external organization or production account was tested.
records.attribution: Johnny performed and analyzed the controlled test. Claude Code later moved the resolved case to Closed at his request, preserving his analysis.
records.impact: The test bypassed the intentionally vulnerable portal login. This demonstrates the lab application weakness, not compromise of Active Directory or another service.
records.timeline:
October 6: the controlled login succeeded and Johnny investigated the alert.
October 13: Claude Code completed the requested transition to Closed.
records.evidence: Private source records: FakeCorp auth.log and matching Wazuh/Splunk detection. Raw request input and attachments are omitted from this public excerpt.
records.queries: Compare the application authentication outcome with the submitted input pattern and the SIEM rule. A successful HTTP response alone is not proof of successful authentication.
records.detection: The successful-login rule captured the combination of suspicious input and an application-reported successful login.
records.containment: No isolation was performed. The declared lab application remains deliberately vulnerable for scoped practice.
records.eradication: No application repair was claimed by this detection test.
records.recovery: No recovery change was required or claimed.
records.conclusion: Expected Test Activity. The controlled SQL-injection input produced a successful login and the intended detection.
records.validation: Johnny observed the successful login and matching rule 100345 alert.
records.lessons: Separate an attack-looking request from its actual application outcome. A lab intentionally retaining a weakness is different from fixing that weakness.
records.publicWorkCredit: Johnny performed and analyzed the controlled test. Claude Code later moved the resolved case to Closed at his request, preserving his analysis.

records.alertSource: Wazuh rule 92057 via Splunk and LabWatch
records.title: RTD Round 2: encoded PowerShell and a failed HTTPS probe
records.initialAlert: Wazuh rule 92057 detected an encoded PowerShell child process on WS01. The original Sysmon process-start record was 182293.
records.observedFacts: Johnny decoded the command without executing the decoded text. It was an availability probe run by a scheduled task under LOCAL SERVICE. Its report showed a failed request to an IP-based HTTPS URL. He changed only the endpoint to the service hostname and reran the same task.
records.scope: The dedicated WS01 exercise task and its read-only HTTPS dependency on SRV01. Task-discovery guidance was provided during the exercise.
records.attribution: Johnny performed the investigation and endpoint repair. Codex reviewed the fresh same-account result, closed the case at his request and performed the subsequent scoped cleanup.
records.impact: The dedicated availability check failed. No wider outage or data-access impact was established.
records.timeline:
October 14: the native encoded-PowerShell alert opened the case.
October 15: Johnny corrected the endpoint and obtained a fresh LOCAL SERVICE result.
Codex verified the result, preserved evidence, closed the incident and removed the disposable task and four owned files.
records.evidence: The private case retains the original alert, Johnny notes, task definition, failed and successful reports, file manifest and cleanup proof. Attachment EVD-473CEE2C4386E79E was uploaded and downloaded with matching hashes; attachment bytes are not published here.
records.queries: Decode the recorded command as text; derive the scheduled task from the evidence; compare its account, action, configured endpoint, report time and last result.
records.detection: The encoded-execution behavior was real. Its authorized purpose and the separate configuration failure were established through the investigation.
records.containment: No emergency host isolation or account elevation was performed.
records.eradication: No malware eradication was claimed. Codex removed only the dedicated task, four reviewed files and empty exercise folder after evidence preservation.
records.recovery: Johnny replaced the IP URL with the service hostname, retaining the same task action and LOCAL SERVICE account. The fresh run reached HTTP 401 and exited successfully.
records.conclusion: Benign True Positive. The alert identified authorized encoded execution, and Johnny repaired the scoped availability probe.
records.validation: The fresh report showed LOCAL SERVICE, HttpReached true, HTTP 401, no error and task result 0. HTTP 401 proves an authentication response, not authenticated document access. Codex verified the task and exercise folder were absent after cleanup.
records.lessons: Distinguish TCP reachability, TLS establishment, an HTTP response and authorized application access. Test the original background identity rather than substituting a privileged manual run.
records.publicWorkCredit: Johnny performed the investigation and endpoint repair. Codex reviewed the fresh same-account result, closed the case at his request and performed the subsequent scoped cleanup.

records.alertSource: Wazuh rule 100277 via Splunk and LabWatch
records.title: RTD Round 3: scheduled-task alert and an output-permission failure
records.initialAlert: Wazuh rule 100277 detected a scheduled task invoking an interpreter from the exercise workflow. The primary Windows Security 4698 record was 54654.
records.observedFacts: Johnny traced the task to a local queue-processing script running as LOCAL SERVICE. The failed report showed that input could be read but the output summary could not be written. One explicit Write deny applied to that account despite inherited Modify permission. He removed that exact deny and reran the original task.
records.scope: The dedicated WS01 queue workflow and output directory. A second authorized task-registration event from another exercise was grouped into the same case and separately accounted for.
records.attribution: Johnny investigated and repaired the exact permission defect. Codex reviewed the fresh task, ACL, report, actual output and both grouped source events before closing the case at his request.
records.impact: The dedicated workflow failed to write its summary. No wider business impact was established.
records.timeline:
October 14: the scheduled-task registration created the native case.
October 15: Johnny corrected the specific deny and ran the same LOCAL SERVICE task.
Codex verified the new result and closed the case. The repaired task was retained.
records.evidence: The private case retains Johnny notes, both source alerts, original failed-state evidence, current task/ACL/report readback and a per-file manifest. Attachment EVD-6291CCA02BFC8481 was uploaded and downloaded with matching hashes; attachment bytes are not public.
records.queries: Compare the task creator with its runtime identity. Inspect the actual failing path and applicable ACL. After the scoped change, compare a fresh report, task result, output content and unchanged input hash.
records.detection: The interpreter task registration was real and authorized. The operational fault was a specific output permission, not proof that the task itself was malicious.
records.containment: No isolation or task-account elevation was performed.
records.eradication: Johnny removed only the explicit, noninherited LOCAL SERVICE Write deny. No malware removal or fixture cleanup was performed.
records.recovery: The unchanged task and account read the same input and wrote the expected Items: 3 summary.
records.conclusion: Benign True Positive. Johnny repaired the scoped NTFS permission defect and demonstrated successful execution under the original service account.
records.validation: Fresh LOCAL SERVICE report: InputRead true, OutputWritten true and no error. Task result 0 agreed with the actual Items: 3 output. Input hash unchanged. The repaired task remained idle without automatic triggers at review.
records.lessons: A task creator is not necessarily its runtime user. Check explicit denies as well as inherited allows. Prove recovery with the account and operation that originally failed.
records.publicWorkCredit: Johnny investigated and repaired the exact permission defect. Codex reviewed the fresh task, ACL, report, actual output and both grouped source events before closing the case at his request.

plainEnglish.INC-2026-0108: I tested repeated failed logins against my lab portal, followed the alert into Wazuh, Splunk and LabWatch, and confirmed the incident matched my test. This shows authentication triage and detection validation, not a real-world breach.
plainEnglish.INC-2026-0109: I tested a deliberately vulnerable login, confirmed that the SQL-injection input actually got me in, and matched that outcome to the alert. I kept the finding limited to the synthetic portal rather than claiming the whole server or domain was compromised.
plainEnglish.INC-2026-0140: I investigated an encoded PowerShell alert and found a scheduled availability check using the wrong form of HTTPS address. I changed the endpoint and proved the same low-privilege task could reach the service. Codex handled evidence review, final closure and cleanup; task-discovery guidance was provided.
plainEnglish.INC-2026-0141: I followed a scheduled-task alert to a job that could read its input but could not write its output. I found an explicit deny for the service account, removed only that deny and verified a fresh successful run without elevating the account. Codex reviewed and closed the case; the repaired task was retained.
